html:
The Red Fort in Delhi was the palace of the Mughal emperors for two hundred years. Shah Jahan built it between 1639 and 1648 when he moved his capital from Agra to his new city of Shahjahanabad.

Its walls of red sandstone run for about 2.4 kilometres and stand up to 33 metres high. Inside, along the river side, was a row of white marble pavilions joined by a water channel called the Stream of Paradise. In the hall of private audience stood the Peacock Throne. A Persian verse on its wall reads: if there is a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this.

The fort's later story is the story of the empire's fall:

  • 1739: Nader Shah of Iran took the throne and the treasure.
  • 1857: rebel soldiers made the old emperor their leader (see the Indian Rebellion). The British retook Delhi, tried him in his own hall, and pulled down most of the palace for barracks.
  • 1945: officers of the Indian National Army were tried here.

Since 1947 the prime minister of India has raised the national flag on its gate every 15 August. It became a World Heritage Site in 2007.
